learning_outcomes.text: Analyze and cinematically synthesize mechanisms.
Pose and solve the direct and inverse dynamic problem of a planar mechanism.
Analyze and design rigid and flexible transmissions.
Familiarize with widely applied mechanisms and understand that many apparently different mechanisms respond to the same kinematic principles.
Create kinematic diagrams of real mechanisms as a form of representation and understand the mechanism's operation from such a diagram.

Structurally analyze articulated mechanisms by criteria of nature and number of links or pairs, and by dimensional criteria, thereby describing the degrees of freedom or mobility of the mechanism and the existence or non-existence of dead or return points and their singularities.
Know and develop the concepts, fundamentals, and methods applied for the kinematic and dynamic analysis of planar mechanisms.
Calculate velocities, accelerations, and forces in any planar mechanism, for specific positions of the mechanism and for complete cycles of movement.
Determine the type and dimensions of a bar mechanism to perform a specific function (problem known as mechanism synthesis).
Assimilate the relationships between actions and the movement they produce in machines and be able to recognize the type of dynamic problem associated with each case.
Determine the inertia effects supported by the links or bars that make up the mechanisms.
Correctly include friction forces in sliding, rotational pairs, and rolling.

Calculate the power that a motor driving a mechanical system must have or the power that a brake installed in the system must dissipate, and establish its relationship with the useful power and the power needed to accelerate or brake the entire assembly.
Obtain and interpret graphs of motor torque and resistant torque reduced to an axis, and understand the cyclic operation of a machine, establishing the permanence condition.
Calculate the dimensions of disk and rim flywheels, by the approximate procedure, in order to control cyclic speed variations in the steady operating regime of cyclic machines.
Know the most frequent causes and consequences of rotor imbalance, and use and know techniques for balancing rotating masses in one and two correction planes, applying balancing regulations.
Know and define the key dimensions and characteristics of motion transmissions between rotating shafts (gears, belts, ...).
Determine transmission ratios in ordinary and planetary gear trains and know some criteria preferably used to define the number of teeth.

Describe the role played by cam mechanisms, pointing out their advantages and disadvantages in relation to other mechanisms that achieve the same results, and be able to design the necessary cam profile from the definition of the follower displacement diagram and its typology.
Use software for the analysis, simulation, and design of machines and mechanisms.
Analyze and select information from various sources.
Develop the ability to understand and interpret the results obtained through kinematic and dynamic analysis of mechanisms and machines.

syllabus_topics: Block I. INTRODUCTION TO THE THEORY OF MACHINES AND MECHANISMS
Concept of machine and mechanism, terminology and classification of elements and pairs. Schematization of mechanisms
Kinematic chain. Inversions and derived mechanisms. Mobility
RRRR Mechanism. Grashoff's Law. Dead points
Block II. KINEMATIC ANALYSIS OF PLANAR MECHANISMS
Chapter 4. Introduction to kinematic analysis of mechanisms
Introduction to kinematic analysis of planar mechanisms
Instantaneous centers of velocity: definition and determination of their position
Instantaneous centers of velocity: determination of velocities
Method of relative velocities and accelerations: velocities
Method of relative velocities and accelerations: accelerations
Block III. SYNTHESIS OF PLANAR MECHANISMS
Block IV. DYNAMIC ANALYSIS OF PLANAR MECHANISMS
Chapter 9. Introduction to dynamic analysis of mechanisms
Introduction to dynamic analysis of planar mechanisms
Considerations regarding the practical application of Newton-Euler formulation to mechanism analysis. Resolution of the inverse dynamic problem: matrix and superposition method
Direct dynamic analysis on reduced mechanisms
Friction in rotational pairs. Rolling friction
Steady state. Degree of irregularity. Effects. Concept of GD2
Imbalance in mechanisms. Concept of balancing. Balancing of mechanisms
General conditions for rotor balancing. Measurement of imbalance. Balancing of rotors with known balance
Introduction, classification, and terminology. Displacement diagram
Fundamental law of design and kinematics of cams
Design of planar cams: with roller follower and flat face in translation
Cylindrical gears. Worm-wheel gears. Conical gears
Variation of center distance. Interference. Tooth correction
teaching_methods: Laboratory practices (software for design and simulation, visualization of mechanisms, mechanical systems, and real prototypes)

assessment_methods.method: Group work report (INF), presentation and public defense (PyD), and participation in subsequent debate (DB)
Laboratory practices exam (EXPL) for extraordinary call

assessment_rules: For the ordinary and extraordinary calls in May/June, the global grade is calculated as 0.1*PR + TGR + PA + 0.7*EX. PR is calculated as 0.15*PR1 + 0.3*PR2 + 0.3*PR3 + 0.25*PR4. TGR = INF*Ci + PyD + DB, where Ci is a participation coefficient. PA is calculated as 0.04*I1 + 0.06*I2 + 0.07*I3 + 0.04*TU, with a maximum value of 0.5. For the extraordinary call in January, differentiated evaluation, and Erasmus students, the global grade is calculated as 0.1*EXPL + 0.9*EXTEO. No minimum score is required for any partial evaluable activity. If an activity is not performed, its grade will be zero for the global grade calculation. During the exam, only provided forms from Campus Virtual and a programmable calculator are allowed.
